1	# cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
2	
3	Milestone 1 of a small game where NPCs hold conversations powered by a single
4	local LLM. This first slice is just a chat window with one companion NPC named
5	**Wren**. No world, no movement, no combat — just dialogue. Later NPCs reuse
6	the same `LlmClient` by design.
7	
8	## Architecture at a glance
9	
10	- **One `LlmClient`** owns the only thread that talks to the LLM. Every NPC
11	  submits requests to it and gets replies back through a thread-safe queue
12	  drained on the main thread.
13	- **`Npc`** holds a `Persona` and a bounded conversation history. The history
14	  is capped at 10 round-trip turns so token usage stays predictable.
15	- **`Persona`** is a small struct rendered into a system prompt. "Jim the
16	  pharmacist" and "Jane the random pedestrian #47" are two `Persona` instances,
17	  not two classes.
18	- **Ollama** runs as a sidecar HTTP service. The C++ side just POSTs JSON to
19	  `localhost:11434/api/chat`. Vendored header-only deps (`cpp-httplib`,
20	  `nlohmann/json`) live in `external/`.
21	
22	## One-time setup
23	
24	### 1. Install Ollama
25	
26	- **Linux:** `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`
27	- **Windows:** installer from <https://ollama.com>
28	
29	### 2. Pull a model
30	
31	```
32	ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
33	```
34	
35	About 2 GB. Runs comfortably on any 6 GB+ NVIDIA GPU. Swap to a different tag
36	later by editing `config/llm.cfg` — no rebuild needed. Suggested alternates:
37	
38	- `llama3.2:3b-instruct` — comparable size, different voice.
39	- `hermes3:8b` — bigger, much better roleplay; needs ~5 GB VRAM at Q4_K_M.
40	
41	### 3. Install SFML 2.6
42	
43	- **Linux (Debian/Ubuntu):** `sudo apt install libsfml-dev`
44	- **Linux (Arch):** `sudo pacman -S sfml`
45	- **Windows:** MSYS2 UCRT64 — `pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml`
46	
47	## Build & run
48	
49	Make sure `ollama serve` is running, then:
50	
51	```
52	./run.sh         # Linux / macOS
53	./run.ps1        # Windows (PowerShell, MSYS2 UCRT64)
54	```
55	
56	Either script verifies Ollama is reachable, configures CMake, builds, and
57	launches the game.
58	
59	Or manually:
60	
61	```
62	cmake -S . -B build
63	cmake --build build -j
64	./build/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
65	```
66	
67	## Talking to Wren
68	
69	Type a line, press Enter. The input box dims while Wren is thinking; it
70	re-enables once the reply lands. Press Esc (or close the window) to quit.
71	
72	## Where to look next
73	
74	- `src/Persona.hpp` — add traits, change voice, or define new NPCs.
75	- `personas/companion.txt` — extra system-prompt directives, hot-reloaded on
76	  every launch (no rebuild).
77	- `config/llm.cfg` — host, port, model tag, temperature.
78	
79	## Future milestones
80	
81	- Multiple NPCs in one scene (architecture already supports it).
82	- Streaming token-by-token replies for a snappier feel.
83	- Persistent per-NPC memory across sessions.
84	- Embed `llama.cpp` directly to drop the Ollama dependency.

1	# Embedded LLMs in Game Applications
2	
3	> Topic for `/teach`: how LLMs get plugged into games, what the engineering
4	> tradeoffs are, and how the choices map onto the code we just wrote.
5	
6	---
7	
8	## 1. The concept
9	
10	An **embedded LLM in a game** is a language model whose output is consumed by
11	the running game process — usually to generate NPC dialogue, narrate events,
12	or interpret freeform player input. "Embedded" in this context does **not**
13	necessarily mean the model lives inside the game's binary; it means the game
14	itself drives inference (vs. the user opening ChatGPT in another window).
15	There are three integration styles, and the choice shapes everything else:
16	
17	- **Cloud API call** (OpenAI, Anthropic, Inworld, Convai). The game POSTs JSON
18	  to a remote service. Easy to start, no install on the player's machine, best
19	  model quality. Costs money per token, requires internet, leaks user prompts
20	  to a third party, and adds 200-800 ms of latency per reply on top of
21	  generation time. Inworld and Convai are middleware that wrap this pattern
22	  specifically for game NPCs.
23	- **Sidecar process** (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile, vLLM). A separate process
24	  on the player's machine hosts the model and exposes an HTTP API on
25	  `localhost`. The game stays small; model swaps are config changes. This is
26	  the easiest "fully local" path and what we picked for milestone 1.
27	- **In-process / embedded library** (`llama.cpp`, GGML, ONNX Runtime,
28	  candle-rs, MLC-LLM). The model lives inside the game binary, called directly
29	  through a C/C++ API. Lowest latency, no separate install for the player,
30	  full control over sampling and KV-cache management. Highest engineering
31	  cost: you own GPU detection, model loading, quantization formats, and
32	  thread management.
33	
34	Why this pattern at all? Pre-LLM NPCs used **dialogue trees** — finite,
35	hand-authored graphs of "if player picks option B, NPC says line 47." That
36	scales linearly with writer-hours and produces conversations that feel
37	canned after two playthroughs. LLM-driven NPCs trade authorial control for
38	combinatorial breadth: the same blacksmith can answer a question no writer
39	ever anticipated, in voice, because the persona prompt constrains *how* he
40	talks rather than *what* he can say. The tradeoff is loss of guarantees:
41	the NPC might hallucinate a quest item that doesn't exist, refuse to answer
42	in character, or — without guardrails — start discussing real-world topics.
43	**Persona prompting** plus **bounded history** is the cheap mitigation
44	(what we used); **structured output** (force JSON with allowed actions) and
45	**retrieval-augmented generation** (RAG, where the NPC's "memory" is a
46	searched knowledge base) are the heavier ones.
47	
48	Industry footprint as of 2026: AI Dungeon (2019, the original) ran on
49	GPT-2/3 cloud calls. *Suck Up!* (2023) shipped with cloud LLM-driven NPCs
50	behind a paywalled key. Modders shipped Skyrim and Stardew Valley LLM-NPC
51	mods using Ollama as a local sidecar. Roblox added cloud LLM "assistants"
52	into their creator tools. Nobody has shipped a AAA title with fully
53	embedded local LLMs yet, mostly because consumer GPU VRAM still limits how
54	big a model can ride along with a 6-8 GB game.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## 2. Minimal example
59	
60	The pattern below is the **whole** sidecar-LLM technique in 15 lines. It
61	posts a chat request to a local Ollama process and prints the reply. The
62	real game just wraps this in a worker thread and a reply queue.
63	
64	```cpp
65	#include "httplib.h"   // single-header HTTP client
66	#include "json.hpp"    // single-header JSON
67	using nlohmann::json;
68	
69	int main() {
70	    // 1. Build the chat body. "system" sets the persona; "user" is the player line.
71	    json body = {
72	        {"model", "qwen2.5:3b-instruct"},
73	        {"stream", false},
74	        {"messages", {
75	            {{"role", "system"}, {"content", "You are a gruff blacksmith. Reply in 1-2 sentences."}},
76	            {{"role", "user"},   {"content", "Have you seen any travelers today?"}},
77	        }},
78	    };
79	
80	    // 2. POST to Ollama's local HTTP API. No auth, no keys — it's on localhost.
81	    httplib::Client cli("localhost", 11434);
82	    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");
83	
84	    // 3. Parse the reply. Ollama returns { "message": { "role", "content" }, ... }
85	    auto parsed = json::parse(res->body);
86	    std::cout << parsed["message"]["content"].get<std::string>() << "\n";
87	}
88	```
89	
90	What this example **does not** show but a real game needs:
91	- **Async**: the call above blocks for ~1-3 seconds. A game loop can't sit on
92	  it; you spin a worker thread and poll a reply queue.
93	- **History**: each NPC needs its own prior `messages[]` so context carries
94	  across turns. Without history every reply is amnesiac.
95	- **Bounding**: history grows forever if you let it. Cap to N recent turns
96	  or token-count-trim from the oldest.
97	- **Failure handling**: Ollama might not be running. The HTTP call might
98	  time out. The reply might be malformed JSON. None of that should crash
99	  the game.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## 3. How this maps onto our project
104	
105	Every bullet in the "real game needs" list above corresponds to a piece of
106	code we wrote. The teaching example is what `LlmClient::processOne()` would
107	look like with all the production concerns ripped out:
108	
109	| Concept                | Where it lives in our code |
110	| ---------------------- | -------------------------- |
111	| HTTP POST to Ollama    | `LlmClient.cpp` → `processOne()` |
112	| Persona as system prompt | `Persona.hpp` → `renderSystemPrompt()` |
113	| Per-NPC history        | `Npc.hpp` → `std::vector<ChatTurn> history_` |
114	| Bounded history (10 turns) | `Npc.cpp` → `trimHistory()` |
115	| Async via worker thread | `LlmClient.cpp` → `workerLoop()` |
116	| Game-loop-friendly polling | `LlmClient.cpp` → `drainReplies()` |
117	| Failure → in-character message | `main.cpp` → "[Wren seems distracted…]" |
118	
119	The structural decisions all trace back to one principle: **the LLM is an
120	external dependency that may be slow or absent, so it must be reachable
121	from any NPC through one chokepoint that owns its own thread.** That's
122	why `LlmClient` is a single object the whole game shares — not because
123	"singleton" is fashionable, but because Ollama can only sensibly serve
124	one request at a time on a single GPU, and centralizing the queue avoids
125	each NPC re-implementing the same thread-and-mutex dance.
126	
127	What we deliberately deferred — and why:
128	
129	- **Streaming**: Ollama supports `"stream": true`, which returns one JSON
130	  line per token. Lower perceived latency, more complex client. Add when
131	  the "thinking…" dwell time feels long.
132	- **Structured output**: we don't constrain the reply format. If we later
133	  want NPCs to emit `{"line": "...", "give_item": "rope"}`, switch to
134	  Ollama's `format: "json"` mode and validate against a schema.
135	- **In-process llama.cpp**: the public `LlmClient::submit / drainReplies`
136	  interface hides the transport. Swapping the body of `processOne()` from
137	  HTTP to a direct `llama_eval()` call is a one-file change.
138	
139	---
140	
141	## 4. The actual code (annotated against the concepts)
142	
143	Below is the heart of `LlmClient.cpp` with the concepts from §1-3 called
144	out inline. (The file in the repo has the same code with lighter
145	commentary.)
146	
147	```cpp
148	// Concept: SIDECAR INTEGRATION — game talks to Ollama via plain HTTP.
149	// Same shape as the minimal example, but wrapped in production concerns.
150	ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
151	    ChatReply reply;
152	    reply.id = req.id;
153	
154	    // Concept: PERSONA + HISTORY — every request is (system prompt) +
155	    // (prior turns) + (new user line). The persona makes the NPC stay in
156	    // character; the history makes the conversation feel continuous.
157	    json messages = json::array();
158	    if (!req.systemPrompt.empty()) {
159	        messages.push_back({{"role", "system"}, {"content", req.systemPrompt}});
160	    }
161	    for (const auto& turn : req.history) {
162	        messages.push_back({{"role", turn.role}, {"content", turn.content}});
163	    }
164	    messages.push_back({{"role", "user"}, {"content", req.userMessage}});
165	
166	    // stream=false → one big reply at the end. Switch to true for token-
167	    // by-token streaming later.
168	    json body = {
169	        {"model", config_.model},
170	        {"messages", messages},
171	        {"stream", false},
172	        {"options", {{"temperature", config_.temperature}}},
173	    };
174	
175	    // Concept: FAILURE-FRIENDLY TRANSPORT — bounded timeouts so a hung
176	    // Ollama can't freeze the worker thread.
177	    httplib::Client cli(config_.host, config_.port);
178	    cli.set_read_timeout(config_.requestTimeoutSeconds, 0);
179	    cli.set_connection_timeout(5, 0);
180	
181	    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");
182	    if (!res) {                         // network failure
183	        reply.errorMessage = "could not reach Ollama";
184	        return reply;                   // ok stays false; UI handles it
185	    }
186	    // ... parse res->body into reply.content ...
187	    return reply;
188	}
189	```
190	
191	And the **async drain pattern** — the bit that lets a 60 fps game loop
192	talk to a model that takes seconds to reply:
193	
194	```cpp
195	// MAIN THREAD (game loop): submit the request, never wait for it.
196	companion.ask("Have you seen any travelers?");
197	ui.setThinking(true);
198	
199	// MAIN THREAD (next frame and every frame after): pull whatever has landed.
200	// Concept: ASYNC DRAIN — the worker thread populates a queue; the main
201	// thread empties it whenever convenient. No locks held across rendering.
202	for (const auto& reply : client.drainReplies()) {
203	    auto text = companion.onReplyArrived(reply);
204	    if (text) ui.appendLine({Kind::Npc, "Wren", *text});
205	    ui.setThinking(false);
206	}
207	```
208	
209	The worker thread (also in `LlmClient.cpp`) is the classic
210	condition-variable-driven queue consumer:
211	
212	```cpp
213	void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
214	    while (true) {
215	        ChatRequest req;
216	        {
217	            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
218	            requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] { return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty(); });
219	            if (stop_.load() && requests_.empty()) return;
220	            req = std::move(requests_.front());
221	            requests_.pop();
222	        }
223	        ChatReply reply = processOne(req);   // the slow part: HTTP to Ollama
224	        {
225	            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(replyMutex_);
226	            replies_.push_back(std::move(reply));
227	        }
228	    }
229	}
230	```
231	
232	Two separate mutexes (one for requests, one for replies) is intentional:
233	producer and consumer don't contend, and the main thread can drain replies
234	without ever blocking the worker mid-call.
